## Applied Finance<br>MGMT 648-3, Fall 2026 {.unlisted}

#### Instructor

[Kerry Back](https://kerryback.com)<br>
[kerry.e.back@rice.edu](mailto:kerry.e.back@rice.edu)<br>
J. Howard Creekmore Professor of Finance and Professor of Economics


#### Course Description

This course develops skills for applying the core concepts of finance in real
world settings. Building on core Finance, it provides extensive opportunity to
implement finance theory at a practical level, using spreadsheets and AI as the
analysis tools.

Two questions run through the term: whether a company should make a particular
investment, and what a whole business is worth. Both use the same machinery, and
the course builds it in that order — project cash flows, the decision rules,
and simulation, then free cash flow from the financial statements and the
valuation of a company by discounted cash flow and by comparison with its
peers. The last full day turns to portfolio management: mean-variance
optimization, and the cost of capital that everything earlier took as given.

Discount rates are supplied until October 10, when they are estimated.

Upon completion you should have a deeper understanding of capital budgeting,
financial statement forecasting, firm valuation, and pricing, and be able to
build both simple and complex financial models.


#### Learning Objectives

1. Read a set of financial statements, and explain why income is not cash.
2. Build free cash flow for a company from its filings, two different ways, and
   account for the difference.
3. Analyze a capital investment in incremental terms: sales taken from an
   existing product, savings from equipment that replaces labor, and the cost of
   using an asset the company already owns.
4. Apply NPV, IRR, and payback, and choose among mutually exclusive
   alternatives — continuing, abandoning, or expanding.
5. Simulate an investment and report a distribution of outcomes rather than a
   single number.
6. Value a company by discounted cash flow, and cross-check that value against
   multiples of comparable firms.
7. Construct a mean-variance frontier and find the global minimum variance and
   tangency portfolios, with and without short-sale constraints.
8. Estimate a cost of capital using the CAPM and a weighted average.
9. Direct an AI to build a working model, and check what it gives back.


#### Meeting Schedule

Six dates. The two Saturdays meet in person and run 2:00 – 6:30 PM, with
breaks. The four Thursday evenings run 8:30 – 10:00 PM on Zoom.

| Date | Time | Where | Topic |
|:--|:--|:--|:-----|
| Thu, Aug 27 | 8:30–10:00 PM | Zoom | Course overview. Excel and AI |
| Sat, Sep 12 | 2:00–6:30 PM | In person | Capital budgeting |
| Thu, Sep 17 | 8:30–10:00 PM | Zoom | Free cash flow, and forecasting it out |
| Thu, Oct 1 | 8:30–10:00 PM | Zoom | Terminal values and multiples |
| Sat, Oct 10 | 2:00–6:30 PM | In person | Portfolio management |
| Thu, Oct 15 | 8:30–10:00 PM | Zoom | Final presentations |

The two Saturdays are working sessions built around cases. Bring a laptop.

September 12 is capital budgeting end to end: what counts as incremental, how
inflation is handled, how competing projects are ranked, what to do when the
decision arrives later than the money, and how to report a distribution rather
than a single number. It is worked through cases at the keyboard.

October 10 is portfolio management: the mean-variance frontier, the global
minimum variance and tangency portfolios with and without short-sale
constraints, and then the CAPM and the weighted average cost of capital.

September 17 forecasts free cash flow the long way, running it out thirty years
with no terminal value at all. October 1 replaces those thirty years with a
perpetuity formula, then with a multiple, and then asks what is left if you use
the multiple on its own.


#### Your Company

Each of you is assigned one company at the start of the term and keeps it
throughout. Free cash flow, beta, valuation, and multiples are all computed for
that company.



#### Materials

Nothing to buy.

Ivo Welch's [Corporate Finance](https://corpfin.ivo-welch.org/read/) is the
reading, free by the chapter from the author's site.

[learn-investments.rice-business.org](https://learn-investments.rice-business.org)
is an interactive site I maintain. We will use it in class for portfolios.

Company filings come from [SEC EDGAR](https://www.sec.gov/edgar). Industry data
and spreadsheets come from [Aswath Damodaran's site](https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/)
at NYU, which he updates every January.


#### AI

An AI environment is provided, running GLM 4.7 in Claude Code with access to financial data,
spreadsheets, and code. It is used from the first session, and assumed in
everything you prepare.

Sign in at [lab648.kerryback.com](https://lab648.kerryback.com) with your netid
and student number. The first session covers working with it: prompting it to produce a
spreadsheet whose cells contain formulas rather than pasted values, and checking
its output against an independent calculation.


#### Grading

Nothing you do outside of class is collected or graded. All graded work happens
in the room, live.

Class participation is scored every session, and on the Saturdays that includes
the work you do at the keyboard.

There are two graded presentations:

- September 12, in pairs, two minutes: a recommendation on the investment case.
- October 15, in pairs, eight minutes: a valuation of both companies.

For both, another pair is assigned to challenge the analysis in the session. The
challenge is graded separately.

Grades are assigned following the JGSB elective grading policy: the class mean
falls between 3.5 and 3.8.


#### Preparation

Every session has preparation, and none of it is graded. The pattern is the same
each time: watch the session video, about twelve minutes, or read its transcript;
compute one number for your company or the case; and arrive ready to defend the number and what it means. Each session opens by
collecting those numbers and putting the range on screen.

#### Honor Code

The Rice University Honor Code applies to all work in this course. The intent of
the Honor Code in this course is to ensure that each student claims and receives
credit for their own efforts. The intent is not to limit the exchange of ideas
through discussion among fellow students. If you have any doubt whether an
activity or resource violates the Honor Code, please contact me. Suspected
violations are submitted to the Rice University Graduate Honor Council.

Use of generative AI is expected in this course.
